'''Elizabeth E. Hood''' is a plant geneticist and the Lipscomb Distinguished Professor of Agriculture at [[Arkansas State University]].<ref name="FacultyPage">{{Cite web|url=http://www.astate.edu/a/parking/staff/people-details.dot?pid=f09896c6-469a-49ec-94af-443219b4930d|title=Dr. Elizabeth E. Hood|first=Arkansas State|last=University|website=www.astate.edu|access-date=2020-06-16|archive-date=2020-06-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200617014746/http://www.astate.edu/a/parking/staff/people-details.dot?pid=f09896c6-469a-49ec-94af-443219b4930d|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2018, she was elected a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="AAAS">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-honors-accomplished-scientists-2018-elected-fellows|title=AAAS Honors Accomplished Scientists as 2018 Elected Fellows|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref>

== Education and career ==

Elizabeth Hood was born in 1952.<ref name="mastersthesis">{{cite web | website=okla-am.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com | url=https://okla-am.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/f/i1vgi9/OKSTAT_ALMA21175359830002681 | language=it | access-date=2020-06-17 }}{{Dead link|date=March 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> She attended the University of Oklahoma earning a BA in sociology in 1974. In her masters she switched to botany, studying the biochemistry of a cyanobacteria (''[[Anabaena variabilis]]'').<ref name="mastersthesis" /> After completing her masters, she moved to [[Washington University in St. Louis]], where she studied the natural plant genetic engineering capabilities of ''[[Agrobacterium tumefaciens]]'' as a PhD student, and studied with [[Mary-Dell Chilton]] and [[Robert Fraley]].

From 1988 to 1994, she was an assistant professor of biology at [[Utah State University]]. After that, she worked at Pioneer Hi-Bred, and later at ProdiGene. In 2003, she became a program manager at the National Science Foundation.<ref name="biobased">{{Cite web|url=http://www.biobasedsolutions.org/#!about-us-page|title=biobased|website=www.biobasedsolutions.org|access-date=2020-06-16|archive-date=2020-01-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200129105353/http://www.biobasedsolutions.org/#!about-us-page|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2004, she was hired at Arkansas State University.<ref name="FacultyPage" /> In 2008, she was appointed the Lipscomb Distinguished Professor of Agriculture.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gwis.org/page/honorary_members|title=Honorary Members - Graduate Women In Science|website=www.gwis.org}}</ref>

== Research ==

During her time at Washington University in St. Louis, Elizabeth Hood created the ''Agrobacterium'' strain [[EHA101]], which is widely used in plant transformation.<ref name=hood1986>{{cite journal |author1=Hood, E.E. |author2=Helmer, G.L. |author3=Fraley, R.T. |author4=Chilton, M.D. |name-list-style=amp| title=The hypervirulence of Agrobacterium tumefaciens A281 is encoded in a region of pTiBo542 outside of T=DNA. | journal=Journal of Bacteriology | volume=168 | pages=1291–1301 | year=1986 |issue=3 |doi=10.1128/jb.168.3.1291-1301.1986 | pmid=3782037 | pmc=213636 |bibcode=1986JBact.168.1291H }}</ref><ref name=sciaky1>{{cite journal |author1=Sciaky, D. |author2=Montoya, A.L. |author3= Chilton, M.-D. |s2cid=205272224 |name-list-style=amp| title=A DNA transformation-competent Arabidopsis genomic library in Agrobacterium | journal=Nature Biotechnology | volume=9 | pages=963–967 | year=1991 |issue=10 | doi=10.1038/nbt1091-963 |pmid=1368724 }}</ref>
